Backer of bond is also co-founder of immunology institute
The billionaire (https://www.forbes.com/profile/gary-michelson/) co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, Gary K. Michelson, is one of the two ultrawealthy chief backers of Proposition 38 (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf). The institute first became a nonprofit in 2022. Michelson has given it at least $120 million since then. Michelson is the board chair of the institute, which is housed at a research center owned by UCLA (https://www3.research.ucla.edu/research-park).
Prop. 38’s language allocates half the bond money to one unnamed nonprofit that must meet very specific criteria:
It’s a nonprofit founded before 2025;
It focuses on immunology and immunotherapy research rather than research broadly;
It’s affiliated with a University of California campus with a medical center that serves a minimum number of patients. Currently only UCLA meets that threshold;
It must meet a minimum square footage requirement for the size of the research institute;
It received a minimum dollar amount in donations from funders, including for specific research endeavors.
A UCLA spokesperson, Phil Hampton, confirmed that among all nonprofit entities affiliated with UCLA, only the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy could satisfy the stipulations of Prop. 38.
The website (https://yeson38.com/supporters-list/) supporting the proposition touts it as an effort to award grant dollars to scientists working on drug therapies for incurable diseases, but makes no mention of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy as a likely recipient of half the bond revenue. Michelson and a nonprofit that he founded, the Michelson Center For Public Policy, donated (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1485847&view=late1) at least $8.2 million to the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign. Another campaign donor and institute co-founder, Meyer Luskin, has given (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1485847&view=late1) at least $5 million.
A former science research administrator publicly opposes the proposition. Robert Kaplan was an associate director at the federally funded National Institutes of Health — the world’s largest public funder of biomedical research. He said concentrating half the funding to one unnamed institute is unfair. “There is a lot of talent in immunology, immunotherapy research in California,” he said in an interview. “All the institutions are scrambling, and so tracking a huge portion of it to one institution, I think, is a bad idea.”
Kaplan also worries the bond measure is too focused on one discipline —immunotherapy — at theexpense of a wider array of biomedical research (https://amp.sacbee.com/opinion/op-ed/article315629674.html). He’s currently a senior scholar at the Stanford University School of Medicine’s Clinical Excellence Research Center.
The Michelson Center for Public Policy, where Michelson is the director, has given (https://calmatters.org/about/funding/#:~:text=Michelson%20Center%20for%20Public%20Policy) between $1,000 and $9,900 to CalMatters.
The potential for cures through immunotherapies is huge because most diseases involve the immune system, the bond measure backers say. California science research has been rocked by funding cuts ordered by the White House that led to hundreds of cancelled federal grants. While many of those grants were restored (https://calmatters.org/education/higher-education/2026/07/research-grants-california-2/), the Yes on Proposition 38 campaign says ongoing federal funding instability necessitates state investment in immunology and immunotherapies.
Should Prop. 38 pass, bond payments will cost taxpayers $500 million annually for 25 years (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2025/250488.pdf), bringing the cost of the $8.4 billion bond to more than $12 billion, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office. The office said costs to the state may be less if the drug therapies developed through the bond’s research funding generate profits that are then routed back to California’s coffers.
What bond backer says
CalMatters presented its findings to the The Yes on 38 (https://yeson38.com/) campaign. In a lengthy email response, Claudia Briggs, the campaign’s spokesperson, said Prop. 38’s language isn’t uniquely tailored to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. She defended the detailed eligibility criteria written into the bond proposition.
“We wrote the measure to ensure a highly qualified nonprofit could receive funding,” she wrote. “We can’t speak to the specific institutes that may or may not qualify across California.”
Briggs wrote that the eligibility criteria were “intentionally designed to ensure that whichever institute is selected is prepared to accelerate lifesaving research immediately while maintaining the highest standards of scientific quality, accountability, and stewardship of public funds.”
She explained that the eligibility criteria were crafted to “ensure the selected institute is primarily focused on immunology and immunotherapy research, already has significant resources before receiving bond funds, has an adequate physical facility to accommodate multiple labs and research programs, and has an existing close working relationship with at least one UC campus in order to establish the foundation for the cross-collaboration that will be important to the success of the measure.”
Drugs created through research funded by the bond would have to be discounted at 20% for California residents and 10% of any revenue from the drugs developed through bond-funded research would go back to the state’s general fund. If the revenues repay what the state spent on the bond and there’s money left over (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=13), the spare cash would return to the special account supporting the goals of the bond.
The bond measure language says that if no institute qualifies, the California Department of Public Health can adjust the criteria to select a winning institute.
How the bond seemingly points to one institute
The bond proposition language says that the institute receiving the $4.2 billion must be affiliated with a University of California campus housing a medical center with more than 3.5 million outpatient visitors and at least 35,000 inpatient admissions.
According to the UC’s latest fiscal audit (https://www.ucop.edu/uc-controller/financial-reports/systemwide-reports/medical-center-reports/24-25/medical-center-report-2025.pdf#page=30), only the UCLA medical center and its affiliated sites registered more than 3.5 million outpatient visits in 2025, with 4.1 million visits. UC San Francisco came in second with 3.4 million visits. UCLA’s website says its medical system admits at least 46,000 people for inpatient care (https://www.uclahealth.org/discover/about).
Based on that criteria, only an institute affiliated with UCLA is presently eligible for the $4.2 billion fund.
The bond measure also requires that the research entity measures at least 200,000 square feet and has a “primary” purpose of “conducting research in the fields of immunology and immunotherapy.” Press releases (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/michelsons-give-120-million-gift-to-ucla-immunology-immunotherapy) from 2024indicate (https://www.michelsonmedicalresearch.org/news/california-institute-for-immunology-and-immunotherapy-new-ucla-research-park) that the institute will occupy between 360,000 and 500,000 square feet of space on UCLA-owned property.
The institute’s stated purpose is to be an (https://www.calimmunology.org/) “invention factory” for “life-saving drugs, vaccines, diagnostics” and to “end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” It initially received (https://www.michelsonmedicalresearch.org/news/ucla-receives-120-million-gift-from-alya-and-gary-michelson-ciii#:~:text=%24200%20million%20appropriation%20from%20the%20state%20of%20California) $200 million in support from the state budget that helped to secure (https://calmatters.org/newsletter/california-legislature-first-day/#:~:text=In%20other%20higher%20education%20news%3A) the UCLA research space.
One of the other requirements of Prop. 38 is that the nonprofit receiving the $4.2 billion be an entity that’s received at least $250 million in philanthropic support. The California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy has received a reported $250 million (https://labusinessjournal.com/special-reports/bioscience-institute-takes-shape/#:~:text=Private%20donation%20commitments%20have%20totaled%20%24250%20million%20to%20date%2C%20primarily%20from%20the%20six%2Dmember%20board.).
Another bond measure requirement is that top officials from the affiliated UC campus sit on the unnamed institute’s board (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=7). Four top UCLA administrators are listed on the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy’s board of directors, including the campus chancellor, Julio Frenk, and the school’s vice chancellor for research, Roger Wakimoto. The institute’s webpage, labeled “Board of Directors,” lists the senior UCLA personnel as “UCLA Board of Directors.” At least four UCLA officials must sit on the institute’s fiduciary board, according to a 2023 term sheet (https://regents.universityofcalifornia.edu/regmeet/aug23/h3attach1.pdf#page=3)of the affiliation agreement between UCLA and the institute. The UCLA personnel are named as directors in the institute’s most recent Form 990 tax filing (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093/202631219349301013/full).
Prop. 38 is highly specific about two donations that must be at least $50 million each that seem to only apply to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The bond language says one donation is to support “a rapid vaccine development program” and the other supports “a microbiome research program.”
Michelson and his wife donated $50 million to two research programs with near-verbatim descriptions that match the bond language as part of their $120 million contribution to the institute, according toa press release (https://www.garykmichelson.org/blog/ucla-receives-120-million-gift-from-alya-and-gary-michelson-for-new-california-institute-for-immunology-amp-immunotherapy). The microbiome research will be conducted in collaboration with the UCLA Goodman-Luskin Microbiome Center, which Luskin and his wife helped establish through a $20 million donation they made with another couple (https://www.uclahealth.org/news/release/ucla-receives-20-million-establish-goodman-luskin-microbiome).
Other grants limited to select researchers
While an unnamed institute is to receive half the money from Prop. 38, the other half will be meted out to a narrow array of public and nonprofit-based researchers in California through a competitive grant application process.
A council selected by the chancellors of seven of the 10 UC campuses, officials from other universities and nonprofit researchers will select the winning grant proposals (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf#page=10). The three UC

Prop. 38 was brazenly written to funnel half of this measure's $8.4 billion to a single institute at UCLA. The billionaire co-founder of that institute is the chief backer of this initiative.
By Mercury News & East Bay Times Editorial Boards (https://www.mercurynews.com/author/mercury-news-east-bay-times-editorial-boards/)
PUBLISHED: October 13, 2026 at 6:00 AM PDT | UPDATED: October 13, 2026 at 4:19 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Immunology and immunotherapy research are good things.
Does that mean Californians ought to approve $8.4 billion in bonds to approve a plan developed outside the legislative process? That’s what backers of Proposition 38 on the November ballot believe needs to be done to “accelerate research to save lives.”
But as always, it’s important to check the fine print.
Half of the funds would be doled out as competitive research grants. But then there’s the other half, which the measure details must go to “a single nonprofit medical research institute” that meets very particular requirements.
Among other requirements, the institute must have “an affiliation agreement, entered into not later than January 1, 2025, that creates an affiliation relationship with a campus of the University of California,” be on a campus that “has a public health care system that consists of one or more hospitals and that conducts its own clinical trials” and be “not less than 200,000 square feet in size.” In addition, the health care system affiliated with the campus must also have “a hospital and clinic volume of greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year.”

This level of precision excludes “all but one institute in the entire state: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition,” according to a CalMatters investigation. The billionaire co-founder of the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy is Gary K. Michelson, who is also the chief backer of the Prop. 38 campaign.
While we have issues with most kinds of ballot-box budgeting, the measure should have been more honest and direct with voters. That’s why a proposed ballot measure to fund research that had gone through the public hearing process via the Legislature or a bond measure issuing solely competitive grants would be preferable to this sort of measure, which was drafted by interested parties who can’t or won’t just say what they’re doing.
Backers also argue Prop. 38 will in the end pay for itself because companies that make drugs made possible by this research would have to give back 10% of their earnings to help pay back the bond. “The bonds will be repaid with interest, relatively quickly,” backers said. If that were so, we don’t see what’s stopping the billionaires backing this initiative from privately funding immunology research. If it’s truly a money-making enterprise, private investors will certainly be interested.
Both Dr. Robert Kaplan, a retired professor of health policy at UCLA, and David Panush, president of California Health Policy Strategies, are avid backers of medical research investment in our state. But they are co-chairing the No on Prop. 38 campaign because they say a huge bond is the wrong way to fund research. They decry Washington’s failure to back science, but say “federal cuts are no excuse to put billions in medical research spending on California’s credit card. We should fight to restore federal funding — not force California taxpayers to cover Washington’s retreat.”
Kaplan, who was an executive at the National Institutes of Health, notes that the promise to pay the state back from medical profits is an empty one, which would at best happen decades hence. Panush notes that similar promises from 2004’s stem cell research bond measure amounted to less than 1% of its cost (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2019/190611.pdf), which voters should keep in mind whenever they hear proponents of Prop. 38 declare this time will be different.
Finally, it’s important to remember this measure isn’t free. The Legislative Analyst’s Office reports that repaying the bond will require $500 million to $600 million in spending out of the state general fund for 20 years. That’s money that could be used to tackle homelessness, public safety or take pressure off of taxpayers the next time Sacramento looks for a tax hike. Or, if proponents of Prop. 38 really had a strong case, that amount could also go toward direct funding, without costly interest payments, of immunology research.
No matter how one looks at it, Prop. 38 makes little sense unless your research institution expects to get a windfall of public funds. Vote “no” on Prop. 38.

Proposition 38 is a sleeper on the ballot. California voters should beware | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 24, 2026 2:20 PM
A laboratory technician works at a lab in Folsom in 2020. Proposition 38 would allow California to borrow $8.4 billion to support immunology research, half of which would go to a single nonprofit immunology research institute affiliated with the University of California.
DANIEL KIM
Sacramento Bee file
The search for medical interventions that can bolster our immune systems (https://www.niaid.nih.gov/research/immune-system-overview) to kill deadly diseases such as cancer is one of the most exciting fields in research. It’s why there is bipartisan support in Congress to spend roughly $2 billion annually in pursuit of cures once thought impossible.
Yet here in California, there is a proposed $8.4 billion bond on the ballot to fund immunology and immunotherapy research that is both too big and too flawed to seriously consider. Proposition 38 i (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)s being underwritten by the backer of an institute affiliated with UCLA that wants to exempt itself from public-records laws.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117396.html)
This is no way to invest public funds in research, and even if it were, no state can afford to replace the federal government’s role in primary research. California voters shouldn’t pretend otherwise. The collective editorial boards of The Sacramento Bee, (https://www.sacbee.com/)Modesto Bee, (https://www.modbee.com/) Merced Sun-Star (https://www.mercedsunstar.com/), Fresno Bee (https://www.fresnobee.com/) and San Luis Obispo Tribune (https://www.sanluisobispo.com/) urge a “No” vote on Prop. 38.
The National Institutes of Health funds 332 different (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/) condition, research and disease categories. Prop. 38 asks Californians to fund a very narrow slice of the broader medical research spectrum. And it does so in a remarkably underhanded way.
The measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) guarantees half the money to an institute tied to a campus healthcare system with a workload volume “greater than 35,000 inpatient admissions and 3,500,000 outpatient visits each year.”
That uniquely describes UCLA and an affiliated institution, the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. (https://www.calimmunology.org/) It is backed by a billionaire physician and inventor, Gary K. Michelson. He is the money behind Prop. 38.
The institute’s web page boasts extraordinary goals — “to end disease as we know it within our lifetime.” But the public paper trail on this organization is thinner than ice.
Itslatest tax form reports (https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/872786093/202631219349301013/full) a fund balance of less than $20 million. The institute’s president reported to the Internal Revenue Service that his job required only two hours of work a week. And we’re supposed to trust this institute with $4.2 billion of our money?
It gets worse. Prop. 38 states: “The institute shall not be deemed a public agency for any purpose under state law …” This fine print is a bombshell.
It means we, the paying public, would learn precious little about how this institute operates. The California Public Records Act and other transparency laws would not apply. Today’s shell of an institute wants to become tomorrow’s billion-dollar black box.
Funding public research should not be a popularity contest. Immunology and immunotherapy are important, but so are countless other fields of medical research.
That is why it makes sense to maintain a national approach to health research rather than create a flavor-of-the-month club in California and other states. Whatever President Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk have done or said, a bipartisan coalition in Congress continues to fund federal research.
The leadership of the University of California system should be ashamed to be associated with such a secretive approach to conducting publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 is a sleeper on a crowded ballot, preying on Californians’ goodwill to spend billions that would otherwise go toward running the state. This measure is not a cure. It is a warm-and-fuzzy-sounding initiative designed to keep the public in the dark.

PROP 38: The Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2038.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Research. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney general title and summary, January 2, 2026)
Measure’s own name: California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative (AG No. 25-0026A1)
Type: Initiated state statute (general obligation bond act)
A vote YES means: The state may sell $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds for immunology and immunotherapy research, repaid from the general fund, split evenly between a University of California-affiliated nonprofit institute and a grant program for California public and nonprofit institutions.
A vote NO means: The state does not borrow this money, and there is no new dedicated state funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy research.
Sponsor/proponent: Dr. Gary K. Michelson, the retired spinal surgeon and philanthropist who filed and financed the initiative. Legal filings handled by Olson Remcho, LLP.
On the ballot because: Citizen initiative. Entered circulation January 2, 2026, needed 546,651 valid signatures (5 percent of the 2022 gubernatorial vote), and qualified for the November 3, 2026, ballot in July 2026.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0026A1 (Immunology), Office of the Attorney General (pdf) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20(Immunology).pdf)
LAO analysis: Immunology and Immunotherapy, Initiative 25-0026, Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 38 would let the state borrow $8.4 billion by selling general obligation bonds and spend it on immunology and immunotherapy research, the fields that use the body’s own immune system to fight disease. Half of the money would fund a single nonprofit medical research institute affiliated with the University of California, chosen by the California Department of Public Health under criteria written into the measure. The other half would pay for competitive grants to California-based public and nonprofit universities and research institutions.
The measure directs where much of the money must go. It requires that over $4 billion be dedicated to research on cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s disease. It bars any award to for-profit companies or drug manufacturers. It caps state administrative spending at 2 percent and requires that 98 percent of funds go to research and development of cures.
Two provisions are meant to give taxpayers something back. Any recipient that licenses a resulting drug or technology must make it available to California patients at a price at least 20 percent below the national average. And 10 percent of the proceeds from immunotherapies developed with the money must be paid to the state to offset the cost of the bonds, which the measure frames as a loan program rather than a grant program.
This is the same model California used for stem-cell research, first with Proposition 71 in 2004 ($3 billion) and again with Proposition 14 in 2020 ($5.5 billion).
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0026A1, “California Immunology Research and Cures Initiative,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0026A1%20%28Immunology%29.pdf)
Key language:
“Require that any recipient licensing a technology or drug developed with funds from this act make the technology or drug available to California patients at a price that is at least 20 percent below the national average.”
“Require that 10 percent of all proceeds from the immunotherapies developed as a result of this act go to the state to offset the costs of this act, making this effectively a loan program and ensuring that the taxpayers will fully recoup their investment in this vital research.”
What it amends: Adds Division 110.5 (commencing with Section 130350) to the Health and Safety Code, the “California Immunology and Immunotherapy Medical Research Act”. Because it is a statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, though the measure limits amendments to those that further its purposes.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who proposed it? Filed and bankrolled by Dr. Gary K. Michelson, a retired surgeon and philanthropist, through Olson Remcho, LLP. Administration would run through the California Department of Public Health, which selects the UC-affiliated institute [1, Sec. 130351(c),(e)]. An Advisory and Accountability Research Council, made up of the seven UC campus chancellors with medical or research programs plus ten to fifteen additional members, would oversee grant selection [1, Sec. 130355]. A Citizens’ Financial Accountability Oversight Committee would handle fiscal oversight [1, Sec. 130351(a)].
What would it accomplish? A total of $8.4 billion in general obligation bonds, split evenly between one UC-affiliated nonprofit institute and a statewide grant program, with over $4 billion reserved for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research.
Where would it take effect? Statewide. Grants are limited to California-based public and nonprofit institutions, and licensed products must be sold to California patients at a 20 percent discount [1, Sec. 3(b),(i)].
When is it decided? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. Bonds would be issued over time as the program spends the money, with repayment stretching across roughly twenty-five years.
Why are supporters promoting it and why do opponents oppose it? The proponent argues immunology and immunotherapy are on the brink of transformative breakthroughs against cancer and other chronic diseases, and that a dedicated, reliable funding stream would keep California at the front of that science [1, Sec. 2]. Opponents question whether the state should borrow at this scale for research that federal agencies, universities, and private capital already fund.
4. Trade-offs
The core trade-off is cost against uncertain return. The $8.4 billion is borrowed money. The Legislative Analyst estimates repayment of about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years, which comes to roughly $12.5 billion in total payments and, in the Legislative Analyst’s inflation-adjusted terms, about 10 percent more than the amount borrowed. That money is paid out of the general fund, the same account that funds schools, healthcare, and public safety. The measure’s headline promise that this is “effectively a loan program” rests on the 10 percent revenue-return provision, but the LAO is blunt that any such revenue is uncertain and could take decades to materialize, if it arrives at all.
The stem-cell precedent is the guide here because Proposition 38 copies its structure. California has poured billions into the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine since 2004. By most accounts, the science produced real value in training, facilities, and early-stage discovery. But the direct financial return to the state has been minimal. Under Proposition 71’s revenue-sharing rule, the state had received on the order of only a few hundred thousand dollars from funded inventions by the early 2020s, against $3 billion borrowed. The stem-cell agency also drew years of litigation and criticism over governance and conflicts of interest, given a board dominated by the same institutions eligible for its grants. Proposition 38 places the seven UC chancellors at the center of the council that steers the money, which invites the same question about whether the grant-makers and the grant-seekers are too close.
The argument on the other side is that basic biomedical research is a classic public good that private markets underfund because the payoff is distant, uncertain, and hard to capture. The measure’s supporters can point to the fact that the overwhelming majority of drugs approved by the FDA trace back to publicly funded research [1, Sec. 2(g)]. If even one major therapy for cancer or Alzheimer’s emerges, the human and fiscal value could dwarf the bond cost. The 20 percent California price discount and the 2 percent administrative cap are genuine attempts to answer the criticisms that dogged the stem-cell program. Whether those provisions work in practice, and whether the state should take on this much debt to find out, is what voters are deciding.
In addition, California voters have approved numerous general obligation bonds totaling over $50 billion in the last decade alone. One other measure on the ballot this year, Proposition 1, would authorize an $11.25 billion general obligation bond. The state is repaying about $80 billion in general obligation bonds right now. Local borrowing runs larger still. School and community college districts alone won voter approval for $138 billion in general obligation authority over the same period, repaid through property taxes rather than the general fund.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Creates a large, dedicated, multiyear funding stream for immunology and immunotherapy, fields with real momentum against cancers such as melanoma and certain leukemias and lymphomas [1, Sec. 2(c)].
Reserves over $4 billion specifically for cancer, heart disease, and Alzheimer’s research [1, Sec. 3(d)].
Requires licensed drugs and technologies to be sold to California patients at least 20 percent below the national average price [1, Sec. 3(i)].
Builds in accountability language absent from earlier bond programs, including a 2 percent administrative cap, a 98 percent research-spending floor, conflict-of-interest rules, public disclosure, and independent audits [1, Sec. 3(j)].
Could expand California’s biotechnology sector and, if research succeeds, lower future healthcare costs and generate licensing revenue [1, Sec. 2(k)].
Potential risks
The state borrows $8.4 billion and repays about $500 million a year for roughly twenty-five years from the general fund, roughly $12.5 billion in total payments.
The promised taxpayer payback depends on a 10 percent revenue-return provision that the Legislative Analyst calls uncertain and potentially decades away.
The stem-cell precedent shows direct financial returns to the state can be very small relative to the money borrowed.
Concentrating both the institute selection and the grant council within the University of California raises conflict-of-interest and self-dealing concerns similar to those that dogged the stem-cell agency.
Bond debt service competes with schools, healthcare, and other general fund priorities every year for twenty-five years regardless of whether the research succeeds.
6. Open questions
Which institute would the Department of Public Health select, and how closely do the written criteria track an existing UC program such that the choice is effectively pre-decided?
How enforceable is the 20 percent California price discount once a drug is licensed, manufactured, and sold through national distribution channels [1, Sec. 3(i)]?
What is a realistic estimate of the revenue the 10 percent return provision would actually send back to the state, given the stem-cell experience?
Do the conflict-of-interest rules meaningfully separate the grant-makers from the grant-seekers when the same UC campuses sit on the council and compete for the money [1, Sec. 130355]?
With federal and private funding already large in this field, how much of this research would happen anyway without $8.4 billion in state borrowing?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
California has run this experiment before with stem-cell research. It borrowed billions, funded real science, and got back only a trickle of direct revenue. Before you vote, ask whether Proposition 38’s accountability provisions are strong enough to produce a different result, or whether you are being asked to repeat the same bet at nearly twice the size.
This is $8.4 billion in borrowed money repaid from the same fund that pays for schools and healthcare. Do you believe the state should take on that debt to accelerate research the market underfunds, or that this is a role for the federal government, universities, and private capital rather than California’s general fund?

content.thinking:
The clearinghouse clause would put the institute in charge of licensing for all the grantee research, not just the CIII work, which concentrates a lot of control in one private nonprofit. I'm also looking at the start of a clause about grant agreements requiring recipients to offer the institute something, though that sentence is still cut off.

The measure also gives UCLA the chance to join the funded research and the clinical trials, so the institute's reach extends beyond licensing. I'm noting that the council's first chair comes from UCLA and that council funding decisions have to be made after conferring with the institute, which gives the institute a lot of say over the other half as well.

Californians are being asked to vote “yes” or “no” on 14 ballot measures.
One of them is Proposition 38, which, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=38&year=2026), allows the state to take out a $8.4 billion loan for immunology research. Half the money needs to be used on cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease research and only 2% can be used for administrative costs. Also, half the money would go to a research institute chosen by the California Department of Public Health.
Voting “yes” means California can borrow the money. Voting “no” means it can’t.
Supporters of the measure, also known as the Immunology and Immunotherapy Research Funding Initiative, point to the fact that it’s endorsed by a variety of medical associations, like the American Nurses Association of California and the Parkinson Association of Northern California as a way to develop lifesaving therapies and treatments for different diseases.
Opponents view the measure as a way for one of its chief backers, the billionaire Gary K. Michelson, to fund his own research nonprofit — the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy, which is the only institute that meets the measure’s criteria for receiving the $4.2 billion. Opponents also say the money should be distributed to other areas of medical research.
In order to help you understand the pros and cons of the measure, we asked both sides of the proposal a series of questions.
Below are the answers from the Yes campaign, which have been edited only for length and clarity.
For the answers from the No campaign, go here (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-no-on-prop-38-campaign-why-voters-should-reject-the-measure/).
What problem does this measure solve?
Millions of Californians are dealing with the devastating effects of cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, Parkinson’s, multiple sclerosis and other debilitating and deadly diseases for which we still don’t have cures or treatments. At the same time, federal research grants are being canceled, delayed and thrown into uncertainty, putting future breakthroughs at risk.
Prop. 38 provides a stable, long-term investment of $8.4 billion in breakthrough immunology and immunotherapy research to develop more effective treatments, prevent disease and ultimately find cures.
For patients and their families, scientific progress isn’t abstract. It can mean the difference between life and death, between walking independently and relying on a wheelchair, or simply being able to work, care for your family and live your daily life.
Prop. 38 builds a statewide network so California scientists can collaborate and move promising discoveries toward patients faster, giving millions of people hope for longer, healthier lives.

We asked the Yes on Prop. 40 campaign why voters should approve the measure (https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/11/02/we-asked-the-yes-on-prop-40-campaign-why-voters-should-approve-the-measure/)

Why is it the best solution to that problem?
Prop. 38 makes a long-term investment in one of the most promising areas of medical science: immunology, which harnesses the body’s own immune system to prevent, treat and cure devastating diseases.
Immunotherapies are already saving and extending lives (https://yeson38.com/power-of-immunotherapy/) for patients dealing with cancers like melanoma, lung cancer and leukemia. Patients who have been weeks away from dying have received breakthrough treatments that have led to long-term remission.
Prop. 38 brings together California’s world-class universities, nonprofit research institutions and leading scientists in a statewide effort to accelerate breakthrough immunology research, while providing stable funding at a time when federal research dollars are shrinking and increasingly uncertain.
Prop. 38 is supported by leading patient advocacy organizations including The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research, Alzheimer’s Association, ALS Association, National Multiple Sclerosis Society, Prostate Cancer Foundation, Blood Cancer United, GO2 for Lung Cancer and many others.
Why should California taxpayers take on $8.4 billion in debt for medical research?
Prop. 38 is designed to fully pay for itself with no cost to the state or taxpayers. It requires 10% of all proceeds from the licensing of immunotherapies be returned to California to offset the full cost of the bond, including interest.
Prop. 38 mandates that new treatments and cures developed under Prop. 38 be offered to Californians at 20% below the national average.
Preventing and curing the most pressing diseases will reduce long-term health care expenses and save families and the state tens of billions of dollars in avoided medical expenses.
Public funding of medical research has always been a central component of advancements in medicine. Of new drugs approved by the FDA between 2010 and 2019, 99.4% were the result of publicly funded research.
Prop. 38 also includes strong accountability provisions such as annual audits and limiting state administrative costs to no more than 2%.
With the federal government and private companies already spending billions on medical research, why does California need to step in?
Billions in funding cuts to the National Institutes of Health and other federal partners are already putting critical research for cures at risk.
Private companies tend to invest where they see the clearest path to profit, which can leave promising but high-risk research underfunded — especially early-stage work, rare diseases and treatments that may take years to develop. Public investment is essential in filling that gap. It allows scientists to pursue breakthroughs based on scientific promise and medical need, not just commercial potential, and helps move discoveries far enough along to attract additional investment.
The fact is, those suffering from debilitating diseases can’t afford to wait for the market alone to deliver, or wait on the federal government to fund this research. California can continue to lead the way in breakthrough medical research and the development of cures with Prop. 38.
What happens if the research fails to find any new, profitable treatments?
The field of immunology and immunotherapies has already proved to be incredibly promising. Breakthrough immunotherapies have already been developed and approved to prevent and fight cancers like melanoma, lung cancer, certain leukemias and lymphomas, and more.
The global immunotherapy market was valued at about $284 billion in 2024 and is projected to grow rapidly, reaching $1.3 trillion by 2033. Prop. 38 positions California to lead that growth, and requires 10% of revenues from the licensing of successful therapies go toward repaying the bond, covering both the principal and interest. Prop. 38 is designed to pay for itself and create a sustainable funding infrastructure.
The measure also establishes financial protections around successful discoveries, including revenue-sharing provisions designed to return a portion of commercialization proceeds to California.
At the end of the day, curing the most devastating diseases will save Californians tens of billions in avoided medical expenses. And most importantly, it will save lives.

California lawmakers resurrect $7.5 billion research bond to counter federal cuts
By Tarini Mehta
August 28, 2026 5:55 PM
State Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, delivers remarks during a debate at the Capitol in Sacramento on Friday, June 13, 2025. Wiener authored a bill that seeks to place a $7.5 billion bond for scientific research funding on the ballot.
DANIEL HEUER
dheuer@sacbee.com
A multibillion dollar bond proposal that sought to fund scientific research (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316251545.html) amid federal funding cuts failed to meet the June deadline to secure its place as a statewide measure on the November ballot. Lawmakers resurrected the language just before the close of the legislative session this week, aiming now to present the measure to voters in the March 2028 primary election.
At a news conference Friday, Sen. Scott Wiener, D-San Francisco, announced that the governor along with Senate and Assembly leadership had reached a deal on the science bond bill he authored in January. The latest amendment Thursday night shrunk the funding it would provide for science and health research from $23 billion to $7.5 billion. Now, the bill must survive the Legislature before it concludes on Aug. 31 and receive the governor’s signature to advance — steps that Wiener said he was “cautiously optimistic” about.
“This represents a major effort by California to stand up against the attack on science by the Trump administration, which is methodically tearing down federal support for scientific research, and to really triple down on California’s global leadership,” Wiener said. “This is a big win for the millions of Californians that rely on scientific advancement to cure diseases, prevent diseases, treat diseases, improve people’s health and quality of life, to protect people from wildfires, to build the next generation of agricultural innovations, to lower the cost of food, and so on and so forth.”
Senate Bill 895 (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb895) is an effort to backfill federal funding cuts to research under the Trump administration through a bond program. A bond is a type of long-term borrowing to raise money for various purposes. The state obtains the money by selling bonds to investors and agrees to repay it, with interest, per a specified schedule. The proposed program would be used to finance grants and loans to fund research and construct, operate and maintain facilities for that work.
The bill — through the ballot measure — would establish the California Foundation for Science and Health Research to award grants and loans to public or private research companies, universities and organizations in the fields of biomedical, disease prevention, wildfire prevention, and climate, among others. The legislation also mandates that 10% of the funds be set aside for a state research program modeled after the federal Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency and $1 billion be available to the University of California and California State University for construction of research facilities.
The measure has nearly 50 co-authors and strong organizational support, including from the UC, CSU and Stanford University. It is backed by UAW 4811, which represents 60,000 scientists and academic researchers at the University of California.
Loading…
Shortly after Wiener announced the deal on his bill, Nobel laureates Jennifer Doudna and Randy Schekman issued statements supporting the UC-sponsored legislation. Both UC Berkeley professors, the scientists said SB 895 was critical to California’s research infrastructure and advancement of scientific breakthroughs that improve lives and drive growth.
“California’s strength and ingenuity depends on its ability to turn bold ideas into solutions to our most pressing problems,” Schekman said. “That’s why we need to invest in research and continue building on our nation-leading enterprise at UC. SB 895 will help protect the people and discoveries that drive billions of dollars in economic activity and improve lives across our state.”
While Wiener’s science bond is clawing its way onto the March 2028 ballot, a separate but similar initiative will be voted on by Californians this November. If approved by voters,Proposition 38 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316259099.html) will authorize $8.4 billion in state bonds for California-based public and nonprofit universities and medical research institutions to conduct immunology and immunotherapy research.
Half the funds would be allocated to a single University of California-affiliated nonprofit medical research institute and the rest for research grants to other public or nonprofit institutions. In July, CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) reported that the measure was written in a way that likely predetermines the single institute that will receive half the funds. That institute is the UCLA-affiliated California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose prominent donor and co-founder is the chief backer of the proposition. At the news conference Friday, Wiener said he was not worried about Proposition 38 hurting his proposed bond’s chances.
“That ballot measure primarily funds one particular institute. It’s not a broad science policy funding measure, and so it’s just very different, and I don’t view it as a competitor,” he said.

Endorsement: Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years
Proposition 38 on the November ballot authorizes the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy. But half of that money must go to an unnamed nonprofit medical research institute based on criteria that has no bearing on the ability to conduct high-quality, cutting-edge immunology research.
Daymond Gascon/S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 3, 2026
In a California election filled with compromised candidates and mind-numbing tax measures, wouldn’t it feel great to vote for something everyone can agree will make a positive difference in the world?
Proposition 38 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot positions itself as such a balm.
Opinion : This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/emilyhoeven/article/prop-38-california-newsom-22495203.php)
It would authorize the state to issue $8.4 billion in bonds for medical research into immunology and immunotherapy to identify treatments and cures for cancer, Alzheimer’s and heart disease. If any drugs receive commercial approval, California patients would get a 20% discount off the national average price, and 10% of revenue would go to state coffers.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Who doesn’t want to cure cancer and save the state’s budget in the process?
But Prop 38 is no balm; it’s one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years.
The measure requires the California Department of Public Health to give half the bond money — $4.2 billion — to an unnamed nonprofit medical research institute that meets a long and unusual list of criteria, including occupying a minimum 200,000-square-foot space and receiving a $50 million donation for a “microbiome research program.”
These requirements have no bearing on an institution’s ability to conduct high-quality, cutting-edge immunology research. Instead, they’re written so that a lone research center is eligible to receive (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) the lion’s share of taxpayer money: the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
California has many established and well-regarded research institutes — including some that have made significant advances in these fields.
But the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy is not among them.
Instead, it’s a brand-new institute, and its founders include the same billionaires who paid to put Prop 38 on the ballot: Surgeon Gary Michelson, businessman Meyer Luskin and financier Michael Milken, who, in addition to his longtime financing of medical research, (https://milkeninstitute.org/speakers/michael-milken-5) is also known as the “junk bond king.” He was pardoned by President Donald Trump in 2020 (https://www.cnbc.com/2020/02/18/trump-pardons-michael-milken-face-of-1980s-financial-scandals.html) for his 1990 guilty plea to racketeering and securities fraud.
In an endorsement interview, Yes on 38 campaign spokesperson Robin Swanson insisted to us that the institute is “well positioned” to put $4.2 billion to good use, touting initial philanthropic contributions of $250 million (https://labusinessjournal.com/special-reports/bioscience-institute-takes-shape/#:~:text=Private%20donation%20commitments%20have%20totaled%20%24250%20million%20to%20date%2C%20primarily%20from%20the%20six%2Dmember%20board.) and its affiliation with UCLA and its medical center.
But the California Institute for Immunology & Immunotherapy literally has no track record of developing, funding or bringing medical research to market. It isn’t even fully built. Despite already receiving $200 million in taxpayer funds (https://newsroom.ucla.edu/releases/ucla-to-transform-empty-mall-into-research-park) in California’s 2022-2023 budget (https://ebudget.ca.gov/2022-23/pdf/Enacted/BudgetSummary/HigherEducation.pdf), construction on a “majority” of the space isn’t expected to be completed until 2028, a spokesperson acknowledged via email.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Key leadership positions remain empty. As of this writing, the institute is still searching for a director, the spokesperson said.
It doesn’t even have a public strategic plan (https://www.calimmunology.org/about). When we pressed for details, the spokesperson would only say, “While CIII continues to refine its longer-term business plan, several core elements are complete or well underway.”
The spokesperson insisted that the institute wasn’t involved in drafting Prop 38 and isn’t part of the campaign. But, again, its billionaire co-founders put the measure on the ballot and have raised more than $38 million to support it (https://quickguidetoprops.sos.ca.gov/propositions/2026-11-03/38).
The institute may be playing coy about how it will benefit from Prop 38, but campaign proponents make no secret of where the money will end up.
“CIII is ready to go,” Swanson said, against all evidence.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Swanson and other Prop 38 supporters leaned heavily on the UCLA affiliation to assuage concerns over the institute’s glaring shortcomings.
UCLA is indeed a top research university. But what exactly is the “affiliation” here?
The institute is leasing space at a new UCLA Research Park (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2024/01/03/governor-newsom-announces-world-leading-science-technology-research-center-in-los-angeles/) but will mostly operate independently from the university. An institute spokesperson said the “formal affiliation agreement” defines their “relationship and responsibilities,” including mission and purpose, facilities, funding, intellectual property, personnel and governance. Some senior UCLA leaders sit on the institute’s board of directors (https://www.calimmunology.org/board-of-directors), including Chancellor Julio Frenk, and UCLA “reserves the right to veto actions that it deems will result in reputational harm or contravene the university’s mission,” Phil Hampton, senior director of communications for UCLA Health and the David Geffen School of Medicine, said in an email.
These vague answers do not assuage our serious doubts about the institute’s ability to manage billions in taxpayer funds.
Indeed, the measure also grants the institute “primary responsibility” for negotiating sale and licensing agreements for all drugs developed through Prop 38-funded research — even therapies created by other universities or nonprofit institutions, which would have to compete for the remaining $4.2 billion in bond money.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Funding decisions would be made by a council of representatives from seven of the 10 University of California campuses — Berkeley, Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego and San Francisco — and 10 to 15 other universities and nonprofit research institutions.
But there are red flags here, as well.
The money is reserved for projects at the institutions represented on the council — raising serious conflict-of-interest concerns. (Proponents said council members would have to abide by ethics and conflict-of-interest regulations — although the measure carves out multiple exceptions — and the council and institute would be subject to independent audits and annual reporting requirements.)
Supporters ask voters to look past these issues by arguing that state-level investment is needed because of President Donald Trump’s funding cuts for medical research. But National Institutes of Health funding for immunotherapy research has steadily risen since 2019 (https://report.nih.gov/funding/categorical-spending#/), when it was established as a new category.
Moreover, Robert Kaplan, an opponent of the measure who was an associate director at the National Institutes of Health and formerly led UCLA’s health services program, told us that Prop 38 fundamentally misunderstands how funding top-tier medical research works.
It doesn’t make sense to restrict billions of dollars to just one area of research, Kaplan said. After all, there’s no guarantee that immunology, as opposed to another field of study, holds the cure to cancer or Alzheimer’s. Funding should be prioritized for thoroughly vetted projects that show the greatest promise of making a difference. Limiting the eligibility pool will almost certainly waste money on efforts that lack merit or scientific rigor.
That’s a lesson Californians should be familiar with.
In 2004, voters approved $3 billion in bonds for stem-cell research, swayed by the promise of miracle cures and huge financial windfalls for the state. Those didn’t materialize, a Chronicle investigation found (https://projects.sfchronicle.com/2018/stem-cells/politics/?_gl=1*76rb29*_gcl_aw*R0NMLjE3OTAxMTQ1MzUuQ2owS0NRand6c2pWQmhDM0FSSXNBTG5NdjRuS1U2OEx6Z3BLUndsckVzczNmZTNRNXlnVzNYeFI1VUprUDZqcXljR3h5SzFEQzg2QXBDSWFBa1RLRUFMd193Y0I.*_gcl_au*MTYxMzIzNzI3Mi4xNzg4OTExNzQ5*_ga*MTQ1MTQ5NDU3MS4xNzgxMTM0OTQ4*_ga_56G0ZT3ZD0*czE3OTA4MDgxMDkkbzExNCRnMSR0MTc5MDgwODg5MCRqNjAkbDAkaDA.); in fact, the measure may have actually empowered an uptick in clinics peddling pseudoscience.
That didn’t stop voters from approving yet another measure in 2020 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-Prop-14-no-need-to-15592513.php) authorizing $5.5 billion in bonds for stem-cell research.
About Opinion

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
Let’s not make the same mistake a third time.
There isn’t a family in California who hasn’t been touched by cancer, Alzheimer’s or heart disease. Better treatments and cures cannot come fast enough. We applaud any billionaire who earnestly wants to harness their fortune to fight disease. But if Michelson, Luskin and Milken want Californians to believe that’s their intention with Prop 38, they should spend their own money and come back to taxpayers when their institute actually has some progress to show.

I'm noting the new details here: the SF Chronicle's point that NIH funding for immunotherapy has risen steadily since 2019, when it became its own category. I'm also taking in the criticism of the CIII as a new institute with no track record, no director, no public strategic plan, and construction not finished until 2028, despite $200 million in state taxpayer money in the 2022-23 budget. The measure gives the institute "primary responsibility" for licensing negotiations, and that's where the text cuts off.

I'm checking the rest of the measure's details: the institute's founders, and Sen. Wiener's SB 895, a broader $7.5 billion science bond that's supposed to go before voters in March 2028. I want to confirm the bill actually passed and was signed, since one source treats it as law and an earlier one only describes it as pending.

I'm weighing the case against Prop 38 now, including federal NIH cuts and the Trump administration's freezes on research grants, and I'm setting that against the real value of the research and the fact that half of the funding goes through competitive grants. I'm also comparing how independent sources and editorial boards line up on this, and I'm keeping in mind that I want to give the best case for voting yes before I settle on a view.

I'm weighing whether Prop 38 could offset recent federal research cuts, though it's narrow to immunology and half its money goes to a new institute with no staff or building yet. I'm noting that its accountability rules cap administration at 2% and require audits, but the institute would be exempt from public records and open meeting laws. I'm also checking the math on the state's 10% share of licensing revenue, which I think is speculative.

I'm checking the royalty math next: a 5–10% royalty on product sales would mean the state's 10% cut is well under 1% of revenue, so recouping $12.5 billion would take an enormous amount of commercial success. The LAO says returns could take decades, and the CIRM precedent has produced only a few hundred thousand dollars so far against billions borrowed.

I'm checking the LAO's 2019 analysis of the CIRM precedent to confirm the "less than 1%" return figure, since the pays-for-itself claim depends on it. I'm also noting that the licensing rules could discourage some companies from taking deals, though that seems less decisive than the revenue math.

I'm checking the constitutional provision on naming specific private corporations in ballot measures, since the Article II, Section 12 language seems to bear on how the institute is set up.

I'm going back over the constitutional provision on naming private corporations, since the opponents argue the measure effectively identifies CIII even without naming it, which could expose it to a legal challenge after the vote. I can't recall how the courts have treated "identifies" in past cases, so I'm treating the risk as real but unsettled. I'm also keeping in mind that a "no" vote wouldn't mean opposing immunology research, since SB 895's science bond, the state budget, and federal NIH funding are still available paths.

I'm also weighing whether a "no" vote would leave immunology research without support, since the state budget, the SB 895 science bond, and federal NIH funding would all still be available. Next I want to check the LAO's 2019 analysis of the CIRM precedent, look at how San Diego research institutions are responding to Prop 38, and read Emily Hoeven's column on Newsom's position and the reasoning behind it.

I'm going to check the Yes on 38 FAQ and the Michael J. Fox Foundation explainer for how the supporters answer the single-institute criticism, then look for the Alzheimer's Association statement. After that I'll search for any post-election results and see what the LA Times and San Diego Union-Tribune editorial boards concluded.

I'm now checking the Orange County Register, the Press Democrat, and the Fresno Bee, which are all part of the same chain and so don't count as separate voices. I'm also looking at CIII's own leadership, since the CalMatters piece lists three hires so far: a COO, general counsel, and a scientific advisor.
I have the main arguments now, and next I'll check whether the alternative science bond SB 895 advanced, the earlier stem-cell bond's revenue payback record, and whether results are out.

About This Data
What Is This Data?
Nonprofit Explorer includes summary data for nonprofit tax returns and
full Form 990 documents, in both PDF and digital formats.
The summary data contains financial information from tax returns processed
by the IRS since the 2012 calendar years, as well as data extracted from
digital filings. IRS summary data also includes limited older records. This
data release includes only a subset of what can be found in the full Form 990s.
In addition to the raw summary data, we link to PDFs and digital copies
of full Form 990 documents wherever possible. This consists of separate
releases by the IRS of Form 990 documents processed by the agency, which
we update regularly.
We also link to copies of audits for nonprofit organizations that spent
$750,000 or more in federal grant money in a single fiscal year since
2016. These audits are copied from the Federal Audit Clearinghouse.
Which Organizations Are Here?
Most organizations that have been recognized as tax exempt by the IRS
have to file the Form 990 every year, unless they make less than $200,000
in revenue and have less than $500,000 in assets, in which case they
have to file the Form 990-EZ. Organizations making less than $50,000
don’t have to file either form but do have to let the IRS they’re
still in business via a
Form 990N "e-Postcard," which does not contain financial details. Churches are not required to file Form 990.
Nonprofit Explorer has organizations that are claiming tax exemption in any
of the 27 subsections of the 501(c) section of the tax code. Taxable
trusts and private foundations that are required to file a form
990PF are also included.
Types of Nonprofits
There are 27 nonprofit designations based on the numbered
subsections of section 501(c) of the tax code.
See the list » (https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/annual-electronic-filing-requirement-for-small-exempt-organizations-form-990-n-e-postcard)
Get the Data
For those interested in acquiring the original data from the source,
here’s where our data comes from:
Raw filing data . Includes Employer Identification Numbers and summary financials as structured data.
Exempt Organization profiles . Includes organization names, addresses, etc. You can merge
this with the raw filing data using EIN numbers.
Form 990 documents . Prior to 2017, these documents were obtained and processed by
Public.Resource.org (https://www.irs.gov/uac/soi-tax-stats-annual-extract-of-tax-exempt-organization-financial-data)
and ProPublica.
Form 990 documents as XML files . Includes complete filing data (financial details, names of
officers, tax schedules, etc.) in machine-readable format. Only
available for electronically filed documents. Electronic data
released prior to October 2021 is also available
through Amazon Web Services.
Audits . PDFs of single or program-specific audits for nonprofit
organizations that spent $750,000 or more in federal grant money
in a single fiscal year. Available for fiscal year 2015 and
later.
API
The data powering this website is available programmatically, via an
API. Read the API documentation » (https://www.irs.gov/charities-non-profits/form-990-series-downloads)

Read the full measure ↗ (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf)Official voter guide ↗ (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/38/index.htm)
01 Follow the $4.2 billion
A billionaire is pushing Proposition 38—which unfairly steers $4.2 billion to one institution. The one he helped create.
Proposition 38 appears written to direct approximately half its funding—about $4.2 billion—to a single UCLA-affiliated institution without naming that institution for voters.
California has many world-class universities, hospitals and independent research centers. No institution should be guaranteed billions of taxpayer dollars through eligibility requirements written into a ballot measure.
Public research funding should be awarded through open competition based on scientific merit—not predetermined by the measure’s sponsors.
Bottom line: Californians should not approve a ballot measure that conceals its largest beneficiary while effectively guaranteeing that beneficiary billions of dollars.
02 The guaranteed bill
Proposition 38 would saddle taxpayers with decades of debt, consuming funds that could otherwise support the important services Californians rely on.
Proposition 38 would borrow $8.4 billion, requiring an estimated $500 million to $600 million in annual debt payments for roughly two decades. Those payments would come from California’s General Fund, where they would compete with health care, education, housing, public safety and other essential services.
Proponents suggest that royalties and other returns could help offset the cost. Californians have heard similar promises before, but speculative future revenue is not a responsible basis for taking on billions of dollars in public debt. Taxpayers remain responsible for the bond payments whether the research produces profitable treatments or not.
Bottom line: The benefits are uncertain, but the debt is guaranteed.
03 The wrong way to fund science
Proposition 38 would lock California into fixed funding decisions—and could hinder the search for tomorrow’s cures.
Immunology and immunotherapy are important and promising fields. That is precisely why funding decisions should be made through rigorous peer review and open competition among California’s best scientists—not permanently fixed through a ballot initiative.
Science changes rapidly. The most promising approach today may be overtaken by a discovery in another field tomorrow. Proposition 38 would commit billions of dollars to one scientific area and concentrate half the funding in one institution for years to come. It cannot adapt as evidence, technology and public-health needs change.
California should invest in biomedical research, but it should fund the strongest proposals wherever they originate—not place billions of taxpayer dollars in one institutional and scientific basket.
Bottom line: Let scientists compete to fund the best science. Don’t lock research decisions into the ballot box.
Broad agreement. One conclusion.
A growing coalition says No on Proposition 38.
Across the political spectrum, respected editorial boards, civic organizations, progressive groups and taxpayer advocates agree: Proposition 38 is the wrong way to fund medical research.

$4.2 billion. One preselected institute.
A concise explanation of Proposition 38’s narrowly written eligibility criteria and lack of open competition.
Your browser does not support this video. Judy Heiman · Former Legislative Analyst’s Office
Scientific merit—not institutional favoritism.
Heiman argues that even Californians who favor research investment should demand an open, transparent and accountable structure.
Your browser does not support this video. Dan Carson · Former Legislative Analyst’s Office
A cancer survivor: Prop 38 won’t pay for itself.
Carson connects his support for medical research with his warning that Proposition 38’s repayment promise does not survive scrutiny.
Watch the full press conference (https://votenoonprop38.org/newsroom/press-conference-september-10)
One more question
Why less sunlight for billions in public money?
Despite promises of accountability, the selected institute would not be treated as a public agency under key California transparency and ethics laws, including the Public Records Act, open-meeting requirements and the Political Reform Act.
Public money should come with full public accountability.
Straight answers
Support Research. Fund it wisely and transparently.
Does voting No mean opposing medical research? No. We support biomedical research, including immunology. We oppose a measure that appears to preselect one institution, limits California’s ability to adapt scientific priorities and finances the program with decades of General Fund debt.
Who is positioned to receive the $4.2 billion? The measure does not name the institution. CalMatters reported that its eligibility criteria very likely point to the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy, whose co-founder and board chair is the largest financial backer of Proposition 38.
What if royalties pay back the bond? That is possible, but not guaranteed. The Legislative Analyst says the amount and timing of revenue are uncertain and that offsetting the bond cost could take decades. California’s principal and interest payments would still be legally due.
What should California do instead? Use independent scientific review and open competition to fund the strongest proposals across institutions and fields. Research priorities should be able to change as evidence, technology and public-health needs evolve.

(The Center Square) – A group opposing Proposition 38, a ballot measure in California's Nov. 3 election, is challenging the constitutionality of the $8.4 billion measure.
The proposition would use all of that funding to pay for immunology research, all backed by general obligation bond funds paid for by California’s taxpayers. Roughly half of that $8.4 billion could go to one institution – the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy at University of California, Los Angeles, opponents of the measure told The Center Square. Those opponents are questioning how legal that is.
Part of the problem is the criteria are so specific only one or two institutions can qualify for the money, opponents of Prop. 38 told The Center Square.
“They created these criteria to be eligible to compete, and that eligibility is predicated almost entirely on UCLA’s numbers,” Robert Kaplan, co-chair of the No on Prop. 38 campaign, told The Center Square. “So you’d have to have more than 3.5 million outpatient visits per year, and UCLA has a little bit more than that. UCSF [University of California, San Francisco] is 3.4 [million].”
According to the proposition (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop38-text-proposed-laws.pdf) , the bond money could only go to an institution affiliated with the University of California, the state’s 10-campus public university system. Qualifying recipients would also have to have at least 35,000 inpatient visits at on-campus hospitals and have an immunology and immunotherapy graduate program, among other criteria.
The group sent a letter to California Attorney General Rob Bonta, asking him to look into the constitutionality of the ballot measure.
“Californians are being asked to assume $8.4 billion in general obligation bond debt, with half the proceeds reserved for what appears to be a single, predetermined private institution,” that letter read. “Voters deserve to know whether this arrangement complies with the constitutional safeguards governing initiatives and the use of public funds.”
Editor's Note
This is part of The Center Square's preview coverage of the Nov. 3 general election in California. Ballots were recently mailed to registered voters. The last day to register to vote is Oct. 19. Early voting centers will open Oct. 24 in some counties and Oct. 31 in the rest of the state. And polls will be open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Nov. 3. For more information, see the secretary of state's website, sos.ca.gov (https://www.sos.ca.gov/) . And for early results on the night of the election, see thecentersquare.com/ california (https://www.thecentersquare.com/california/) .
The Center Square did not hear back from the Attorney General’s Office before publication time on Monday.
Advocates of Prop. 38 told The Center Square that the taxpayer-backed bond money for immunology and immunotherapy research is necessary now in the aftermath of federal budget cuts to science and medical research.
“Scientists are losing their jobs, and life-saving medical research has been stopped,” Robin Swanson, spokesperson for the Yes on Prop. 38 campaign, told The Center Square. “So there is a brain drain that has happened in the field of science and research and a race against time. Patients can’t afford to wait, and Prop. 38 will create that stable source of funding for scientists and medical experts so they can do this kind of research.”
Groups supporting Prop. 38, including the Yes on 38 Campaign, the Michael J. Fox Foundation, Alzheimer’s Los Angeles and the American Nurses Association, did not respond to The Center Square's request for comment on Monday.
The opposition's Kaplan said putting this much taxpayer-backed bond money into immunology research limits the ability to fund research in other areas of health science and medicine.
“In terms of the breadth of science, this is very, very narrow and probably reduces the probability that California will independently fund all these other areas of investigation,” Kaplan said. “If you look at funding for immunological research and immunotherapy, funding from the National Institutes of Health is quite robust in this area.”
Expenditures at the federal level in immunological research went up 57% since 2019, Kaplan said.
“Immunotherapy is one of the areas where there has been significant growth,” Kaplan added. “There is a substantial amount of research going into these areas, and it’s not entirely clear that California needs to make this level of expenditure just to keep the research going.”
David Panush, co-chair of the No on Prop. 38 campaign, said he’s not sure how much taxpayers could afford to pay for the Prop. 38 bonds and the bond resulting from Senate Bill 895 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB895) , which places a similar bond on the March 2028 ballot. That ballot measure would authorize $7.5 billion in taxpayer-backed bonds to pay for health and science research, according to previous reporting (https://www.thecentersquare.com/california/article_b3ed7a1a-7a5e-4f5e-8ded-43cc7dd616ce.html) by The Center Square.
“Voters will have a choice,” Panush told The Center Square. “But it would be very costly if the voters were to pass both of them. I just don’t think they can afford both, so they need to choose.”
Officials with the University of California declined to comment for this story. Administrators at UCLA and the California Institute of Immunology and Immunotherapy did not respond to The Center Square's request for comment.

This is the worst measure on California’s ballot — and Gavin Newsom supports it
By Emily Hoeven (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/emily-hoeven/) , Opinion Columnist Oct 31, 2026
Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks in Summerville, S.C., on Sept. 3. His support for Prop 38 and its questionable funding model is not getting the attention it deserves, columnist Emily Hoeven says.
Yalonda M. James/S.F. Chronicle
Gov. Gavin Newsom is catching a lot of flak from Democrats for his opposition to Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php), the billionaire wealth tax.
Yet no one seems to be talking about his backing (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php) of what’s arguably the worst measure on California’s November ballot: Prop 38 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php).
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Read more : Here’s how Newsom is voting on California’s propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php)
Endorsement : Prop 38 is one of the most noxious deposits on California’s political dung heap in years (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-38-money-california-22453646.php)
